claim: The majority of patients receiving cancer immunotherapies will experience only partial response followed by relapse of resistant tumors.
source: Despite the remarkable successes of cancer immunotherapies, the majority of patients will experience only partial response followed by relapse of resistant tumors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about immunotherapy outcomes.

claim: Comparisons of paired primary and relapsed tumors in melanoma and breast cancers indicate that they share the majority of clones.
source: While treatment resistance has frequently been attributed to clonal selection and immunoediting, comparisons of paired primary and relapsed tumors in melanoma and breast cancers indicate that they share the majority of clones.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature and is presented as an established finding.

claim: Tumor cells evade immunotherapy by generating unique transient cell-in-cell structures that are resistant to killing by T cells and chemotherapies.
source: Here, we demonstrate in both mouse models and clinical human samples that tumor cells evade immunotherapy by generating unique transient cell-in-cell structures, which are resistant to killing by T cells and chemotherapies.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data from both mouse models and human samples described throughout the manuscript.

claim: The outer cells in cell-in-cell formation are often killed by reactive T cells while the inner cells remain intact.
source: While the outer cells in this cell-in-cell formation are often killed by reactive T cells, the inner cells remain intact and disseminate into single tumor cells once T cells are no longer present.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inner cells in cell-in-cell formation disseminate into single tumor cells once T cells are no longer present.
source: While the outer cells in this cell-in-cell formation are often killed by reactive T cells, the inner cells remain intact and disseminate into single tumor cells once T cells are no longer present.
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging and culture experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Cell-in-cell formation is mediated predominantly by IFNγ-activated T cells.
source: This formation is mediated predominantly by IFNγ-activated T cells, which subsequently induce phosphorylation of the transcription factors signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) and early growth response-1 (EGR-1) in tumor cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that IFNγ-activated T cells induce cell-in-cell formation.

claim: IFNγ-activated T cells induce phosphorylation of STAT3 and EGR-1 in tumor cells.
source: This formation is mediated predominantly by IFNγ-activated T cells, which subsequently induce phosphorylation of the transcription factors signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) and early growth response-1 (EGR-1) in tumor cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and gene expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inhibiting STAT3 and EGR-1 prior to immunotherapy significantly improves its therapeutic efficacy.
source: Indeed, inhibiting these factors prior to immunotherapy significantly improves its therapeutic efficacy.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo experiments using Stattic inhibitor combined with immunotherapy.

claim: There is a direct correlation between the prevalence of cytotoxic T-cell immunity and improved clinical outcomes.
source: Given the direct correlation between the prevalence of cytotoxic T-cell immunity and improved clinical outcomes (Pagès et al., 2005; Galon et al., 2006; Fridman et al., 2012), most therapeutic strategies are aimed at harnessing T-cell immunity to fight cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Patients experiencing tumor regression following immunotherapy frequently experience recurrence of tumors that are largely resistant to subsequent treatments.
source: However, long-term follow-up indicates that while patients will experience tumor regression, it is frequently followed by recurrence of tumors that are largely resistant to subsequent treatments (Salati et al., 2018; Gide et al., 2018; Gauci et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Tumor cells often express mutated proteins or neo-antigens.
source: As tumor cells often express mutated proteins or neo-antigens (Vogelstein et al., 2013; Schumacher and Schreiber, 2015), it remains unclear why eliciting the full spectrum of T-cell immunity to these antigens is not sufficient to eradicate tumors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tumor cells can edit or lose their targeted antigens, or downregulate HLA molecules to avoid killing by T cells.
source: The main conceptual paradigm suggests that in order to avoid killing by T cells, tumor cells edit or lose their targeted antigens, or downregulate HLA molecules (Khong and Restifo, 2002; Dunn et al., 2002; Gajewski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The presence of immunogenic clones expressing neoantigens and HLA molecules, despite having infiltrated reactive T cells, has been well-documented.
source: However, the presence of immunogenic clones expressing neoantigens and HLA molecules, despite having infiltrated reactive T cells, has been well-documented (Straetemans et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Tumor resistance to immunotherapy can be acquired through tumor cell-intrinsic mechanisms, including loss-of-function of JNK and PTEN, MYC overexpression, and constitutive WNT signaling.
source: Accordingly, tumor resistance to immunotherapy was also shown to be acquired through tumor cell-intrinsic mechanisms, including loss-of-function of JNK and PTEN, MYC overexpression, and constitutive WNT signaling (Zaretsky et al., 2016; Sade-Feldman et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Only about 30% of patients achieve durable objective response following treatment with checkpoint blockade.
source: Nonetheless, only about 30% of the patients achieve durable objective response following treatment with checkpoint blockade (Topalian et al., 2015; Egen et al., 2020; Haslam and Prasad, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Combination therapies of tumor-reactive T cells with immunomodulators such as regulatory receptors blockades are still not sufficient to profoundly improve response rates.
source: Moreover, combination therapies of tumor-reactive T cells with immunomodulators such as regulatory receptors blockades are still not sufficient to profoundly improve response rates (Rohaan et al., 2018; Swart et al., 2016), which strongly suggests that additional escape mechanisms are involved.
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies and leads to an inference about additional mechanisms.

claim: Whole exome and genome sequencing comparisons of paired primary and relapsed tumors indicate that most clones in relapsed tumors are shared with the primary tumors.
source: Surprisingly, whole exome and genome sequencing comparisons of paired primary and relapsed tumors indicate that most clones in relapsed tumors are shared with the primary tumors, suggesting relatively low rates of clonal deletion (Yates et al., 2017; Hao et al., 2016; Gundem et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic studies.

claim: Treatment with TNFα, CD40L, and an antibody against the melanoma antigen TRP1 almost completely eradicated established tumors in all mice.
source: Therefore, when palpable melanoma tumors were injected with a combination of TNFα, CD40L, and an antibody against the melanoma antigen TRP1, tumors were almost completely eradicated in all mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: After about 10 days following immunotherapy, half the mice developed recurrent tumors that were resistant to subsequent treatments.
source: Nonetheless, after about 10 days, half the mice developed recurrent tumors that were resistant to subsequent treatments (Figure 1A, Figure 2—video 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and supplementary materials.

claim: Treatment of melanoma-bearing mice with splenic CD8+ T cells expressing TCR against gp100 or TRP2 melanoma antigens induced significant tumor regression, followed by tumor recurrence in all treated mice.
source: To test if this occurrence represents a broader phenomenon, we also treated melanoma-bearing mice with splenic CD8+ T cells expressing TCR against gp100 or TRP2 melanoma antigens. Both treatments induced significant tumor regression, followed by tumor recurrence in all treated mice (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Recurrent tumors were resistant to subsequent treatment with gp100- or TRP2-reactive T cells.
source: As observed with the previous immunotherapy, recurrent tumors were resistant to subsequent treatment with gp100- or TRP2-reactive T cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Treated mice across all immunotherapies show massive immune-cell and T-cell infiltration.
source: In all cases, immune composition analysis of tumors following the second immunotherapy indicated treated mice across all immunotherapies show massive immune-cell and T-cell infiltration (Figure 1C) with a dominant representation of T-cell clones against the melanoma antigens TRP2 and gp100 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Tumor-infiltrating T cells (TIL) transferred to naive mice prevented tumor growth, indicating their overall activity favours immunity.
source: To test if these tumor-infiltrating T cells (TIL) are active, we adoptively transferred them to naive mice and challenged them with tumor inoculation. In two different tumor models, TIL transfer prevented tumor growth, further indicating that their overall activity favours immunity (Figure 1E-F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Melanoma cells following immunotherapy maintain expression of MHC-I.
source: Next, we assessed changes in immunogenicity of tumors following immunotherapy. Analysis of melanoma cells showed they maintain expression of MHC-I (Figure 1—source data 1), as well as TRP2 and gp100 antigens (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and immunostaining data.

claim: Melanoma cells following immunotherapy maintain expression of TRP2 and gp100 antigens.
source: Analysis of melanoma cells showed they maintain expression of MHC-I (Figure 1—source data 1), as well as TRP2 and gp100 antigens (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Whole exome analysis indicated comparable neoantigen burden across all B16F10 samples from untreated and relapsed tumors.
source: Whole exome analysis (WES) indicated comparable neoantigen burden across all samples (Figure 1I) with the same 25 germline mutations with the highest MHCI affinity (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by whole exome sequencing data shown in Figure 1I and 1J.

claim: RNAseq analyses demonstrated similar patterns of gene expression in cell lines established from relapsed tumors compared to parental B16F10.
source: RNAseq analyses further demonstrated similar patterns of gene expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H) as well as known B16F10 neoantigens in cell lines established from relapsed tumors sorted following effective immunotherapy (Figure 1K, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The majority of neoantigens were shared between relapsed melanoma tumors and their corresponding primary tumor in patients following treatment with checkpoint blockade.
source: To assess the human relevance of these findings, we next plotted the neoantigen burden identified in relapsed melanoma (Zaretsky et al., 2016) and in non-small cell carcinoma patients Anagnostou et al., 2017 following treatment with checkpoint blockade. Consistent with our finding in mice, the majority of neoantigens were shared between relapsed tumors and their corresponding primary tumor (Figure 1L–M).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published patient data shown in Figure 1L-M.

claim: Cell lines established from tumors relapsed following immunotherapy were equally susceptible to the same immunotherapy as the parental B16F10 cells, albeit relapsed more rapidly.
source: Initially, cell lines established from tumors relapsed following TNFα, CD40L and anti-TRP1 were injected to naïve mice and allowed to reach a palpable size. Consistent with their patterns of gene and neoantigens expression, these tumors were equally susceptible to the same immunotherapy as the parental B16F10 cells, albeit relapsed more rapidly (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cell lines established from relapsed tumors were equally susceptible to killing by gp100-reactive T cells as the parental cell line.
source: Indeed, overnight incubation of these cell lines with gp100-reactive T cells indicated they are equally susceptible to killing as the parental cell line (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: B16F10 parental cells and cell lines established following killing by reactive T cells were equally susceptible to T cell killing.
source: We found that both B16F10 parental cells and the cell lines established following killing by reactive T cells were equally susceptible to T cell killing, (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Transient in vivo mechanisms rather than inherited ones govern resistance of relapsed tumors.
source: Taken jointly, these results suggest that transient in vivo mechanisms rather than inherited ones govern resistance of relapsed tumors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that established cell lines lose resistance.

claim: All established cell lines cluster within the same principal components, whereas the expression profile of freshly sorted tumor cells from immunotherapy-treated mice is markedly distinct.
source: In support of this hypothesis, RNAseq analysis indicated that all the established cell lines cluster within the same principal components, whereas the expression profile of freshly sorted tumor cells from immunotherapy-treated mice is markedly distinct (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Most tumor cells that survived immunotherapy organize in clusters of several nuclei surrounded by a single membrane and cortical actin.
source: Confocal analyses indicated that most of the tumor cells organize in clusters of several nuclei surrounded by a single membrane and cortical actin (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy of freshly sorted cells showed a distinct segregation of the membranes and cytosols of the two cells, with the inner cell appearing dense and compacted within another cell.
source: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) of freshly sorted cells further corroborated a distinct segregation of the membranes and cytosols of the two cells. The inner cell was dense and seemed to have been compacted within another cell (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Immunotherapy-treated tumors showed increased prevalence of cell structures where one or more nuclei were surrounded by multiple membranes.
source: Indeed, immunotherapy-treated tumors showed increase prevalence of cell structures where one or more nuclei were surrounded by multiple membranes, especially in sites associated with tumor cell death (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: About half the cells that survived immunotherapy are organized in structures where multiple membrane layers surround the cell nuclei.
source: ImageStream FACS analysis as well as double blind count under confocal microscopy by pathologists indicated that about half the cells that survived immunotherapy are organized in such structures where multiple membrane layers surround the cell nuclei (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: About one third of tumor cells sorted from treated mice were a mixture of both GFP and tdTomato nuclei.
source: To test if this formation was merely the result of incomplete cell division, we injected mice with tumor cells whose nuclei are labeled with GFP or tdTomato, and treated the mice with immunotherapy. About one third of the tumor cells were a mixture of both GFP and tdTomato nuclei (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Single cells sorted from treated mice spontaneously clustered in a cell-in-cell formation during their in vitro culture.
source: Furthermore, monitoring the dynamics of single cells sorted from treated mice indicated that they spontaneously clustered in a cell-in-cell formation during their in vitro culture (Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse video microscopy.

claim: Over time, all cells disseminated into single cells bearing morphological features similar to those of the parental cell line.
source: Over time, all cells disseminated into single cells bearing morphological features similar to those of the parental cell line with no observed cells concomitantly expressing the two fluorophores (Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse video microscopy.

claim: Only T cells—mainly CD8+, and with slower kinetics also CD4+—induce a cell-in-cell formation with the same special characteristics as the ones observed in vivo following immunotherapy.
source: We found that only T cells—mainly CD8+, and with slower kinetics also CD4+—induce a cell-in-cell formation with the same special characteristics as the ones observed in vivo following immunotherapy (Figure 3A, B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: No cell-in-cell structures were observed in Nude SCID-gamma-/- (NSG) mice treated with immunotherapy.
source: Consistently, no cell-in-cell structures were observed in Nude SCID- gamma-/- (NSG) mice treated with immunotherapy (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The same cell-in-cell structures were observed in 4T1 mammary carcinoma incubated with allogeneic T cells, but not in immortalized mammary epithelial cells.
source: We next tested whether this phenomenon occurs in other tumor cell types. Indeed, the same structures were also observed in 4T1 mammary carcinoma incubated with allogeneic T cells, but not in immortalized mammary epithelial cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Immortalized mammary epithelial cells were completely killed by allogeneic T cells and did not form cell-in-cell structure.
source: In contrast, immortalized mammary epithelial cells were completely killed by allogeneic T cells and did not form cell-in-cell structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) suggesting this phenomenon is restricted to tumor cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: There are significant differences between tumor cell lines in their capacity to form cell-in-cell structures, with pancreatic tumors and B cell lymphoma not generating such structures, while almost all colon and ovarian carcinoma tumor cells that survive T cell killing were organized in such structures.
source: We found significant differences between tumor cell lines; on one end are pancreatic tumors and B cell lymphoma, which do not generate cell-in-cell structures, while on the other end, almost all the colon and ovarian carcinoma tumor cells that survive T cell killing, were organized in such structures (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and supplementary figures.

claim: The vast majority of human breast, colon and melanoma tumors that survived killing by pre-activated allogeneic T cells had organized in transient cell-in-cell structures.
source: We then tested whether similar structures are also formed by human cancer. To this end, we incubated tumor cell lines with pre-activated allogeneic T cells from healthy donors. Similar to our finding in mouse cells, the vast majority of breast, colon and melanoma tumors that survived killing had organized in transient cell-in-cell structures (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and supplementary figures.

claim: T cell and myeloid lymphomas as well as glioblastomas did not form cell-in-cell structures.
source: In contrast, T cell and myeloid lymphomas as well as glioblastomas did not form such structures (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and supplementary figures.

claim: Approximately half of patient-derived melanoma cells that survived in culture with their autologous reactive TIL were organized in a cell-in-cell formation.
source: Overnight incubation of patient-derived melanoma and their corresponding reactive TIL, resulted in vast tumor cell killing. Approximately half of the tumor cells that survived in culture were organized in a cell-in-cell formation (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from patient samples shown in Figure 3F-H.

claim: Histological sections of human melanoma xenografts in NSG mice treated with autologous TIL and high-dose IL-2 indicated high prevalence of tumor cells organized in cell-in-cell formation.
source: Histological sections of tumors at this point indicated high prevalence of tumor cells organized in cell-in-cell formation (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: In all stage IV melanoma patients analyzed, cell-in-cell tumor formations were highly abundant in the T cell zone of the draining lymph nodes, but not in the primary tumors.
source: We also analysed histological sections of multiple organs from four stage IV melanoma patients undergoing surgical resection of their primary, and metastatic draining lymph nodes. In all patients, cell-in-cell tumor formations were highly abundant in the T cell zone of the draining lymph nodes, but not in the primary tumors (Figure 3J–L and Figure 3—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis of patient samples shown in Figure 3J-L.

claim: In a patient with untreated recurrent melanoma, the vast majority of cells in the primary tumors were single cells, while recurrent tumors were highly enriched with cell-in-cell formations.
source: In another patient with untreated recurrent melanoma, we observed that the vast majority of cells in the primary tumors were single cells, while recurrent tumors were highly enriched with cell-in-cell formations (Figure 3M).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Tumor-reactive T cells, but not PMA plus ionomycin-activated NK cells or LPS-activated macrophages, express intact granules on their cell membrane.
source: Interestingly, tumor-reactive T cells, but not PMA plus ionomycin-activated NK cells or LPS-activated macrophages, express the intact granules on their cell membrane (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by SEM analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Secreted granules from activated T cells were sufficient to induce cell-in-cell formation in tumor cells.
source: Secreted granules were washed and added to a culture of tumor cells. Similar to activated T cells, secreted granules were sufficient to induce cell-in-cell formation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Extracellular vesicles from activated NK cells, macrophages, immortalized melanocytes, B16F10-derived granules, or commercial latex beads did not induce a cell-in-cell formation.
source: Hence, B16F10 cells were cultured overnight with extracellular vesicles from activated NK, macrophages, immortalized melanocytes (Melan A), B16F10-derived granules, or commercial 1 μM latex beads. However, none of these extracellular vesicles induced a cell-in-cell formation, suggesting this it is mediated by molecules that are highly enriched in activated T cells (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Mass spectrometry identified approximately 400 proteins in purified T cell secreted granules, of which 273 were shared with primary T cell secreted granules.
source: We next analysed the protein content of the purified granules by mass spectrometry. Overall, we identified approximately 400 proteins and out of those 273 were shared primary T cell secreted granules. (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Incubation of T cell secreted granules with tumor cells induced significant cell death.
source: Consistently, incubation of these granules with tumor cells induced significant cell death (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Incubation of tumor cells with gp100-reactive T cells in the presence of antibodies that block the interactions with lysosomes/secreted granules (LAMP1, CD95, or CD63) did not alter T cells capacity to induce a cell-in-cell formation.
source: Most importantly, however, incubation of tumor cells with gp100-reactive T cells in the presence of antibodies that block the interactions with lysosomes/secreted granules (i.e. LAMP1, CD95, or CD63) did not alter T cells capacity to induce a cell-in-cell formation, suggesting that these molecules are also expressed on T cell membranes (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Incubation of tumor cells with extraction of membrane-associated proteins, but not cytosolic or secreted proteins from activated T cells, induce tumor cell-in-cell formation.
source: Indeed, incubation of tumor cells with extraction of membrane-associated proteins, but not cytosolic or secreted proteins from activated T cells, induce tumor cell-in-cell formation (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: T cells activated with IFNγ, and to a lesser extent anti-CD3 plus high-dose IL-2, induce the most cell-in-cell formation.
source: We found that T cells activated with IFNγ, and to a lesser extent anti-CD3 plus high-dose IL-2, induce the most cell-in-cell formation (Figure 4I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The expression profile of IFNγ activated T cells differ markedly than that induced by anti-CD3 or LPS.
source: RNAseq analyses indicated that the expression profile of IFNγ activated T cells differ markedly than that induced by anti-CD3 or LPS, which do not induce cell-in-cell formation in tumor cells (Figure 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: IFNγ-stimulated NK cells and macrophages, but not B cells, could induce a tumor cell-in-cell formation, albeit at a lower percentage compared to activated T cells.
source: We found that IFNγ -stimulated NK cells and macrophages, but not B cells, could induce a tumor cell-in-cell formation, albeit at a lower percentage compared to activated T cells (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Human T cells from healthy donors that were pre-activated with IFNγ efficiently induced cell-in-cell formation in allogeneic tumor cells.
source: Similarly, human T cells from healthy donors that were pre-activated with IFNγ efficiently induced cell-in-cell formation in allogeneic tumor cells (Figure 4L and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Single tumor cells were significantly more susceptible to killing by reactive T cells, compared to that of cell-in-cell tumors.
source: In all assays, we found that single tumor cells were significantly more susceptible to killing by reactive T cells, compared to that of cell-in-cell tumors (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by caspase 3/7 activity assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Pre-incubation of tumor cells with granules isolated from activated B cells and macrophages provided no protection to tumor cells from gp100-reactive T cells.
source: Pre-incubation of tumor cells with granules isolated from activated B cells and macrophages (which do not induce cell-in-cell formation) provided no protection to tumor cells from gp100-reactive T cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Cell-in-cell tumors induced in vitro or in vivo showed only minor regression following administration of immunotherapy, while single melanoma cells were almost completely abrogated following therapy.
source: Cell-in-cell tumors that were induced in vitro have grown slower compared to single tumor cells, but experienced only minor regression following administration of immunotherapy. Similarly, cell-in-cell formation induced in vivo showed only benign response to immunotherapy. In sharp contrast, single melanoma cells were almost completely abrogated following therapy (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Multiple T cells were attached to cell-in-cell tumors and many large pores were observed on the outer cell membrane.
source: We found that multiple T cells were attached to cell-in-cell tumors and many large pores were observed on the outer cell membrane (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by SEM analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Pores on the outer cell membrane were almost completely absent upon co-culture with reactive CD8+ T cells from perforin-/- mice.
source: These pores were almost completely absent upon co-culture with reactive CD8+ T cells from perforin-/- mice (Figure 5D), which have impaired tumor cell killing abilities (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by SEM analysis shown in Figure 5D and functional data in supplementary figures.

claim: The length and duration of the immunological synapse between T cells and cell-in-cell structures showed no reduction compared to single tumor cells.
source: Furthermore, measuring the length and the duration of the immunological synapse under super-resolution microscopy showed that no reduction compared to single tumor cells (Figure 5E–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 5E-G.

claim: The distribution of granzyme B and perforin is almost limited to the outer cell in cell-in-cell tumors attacked by T cells.
source: Immunostaining of T cells attacking cell-in-cell tumors, indicated that the distribution of granzyme B and perforin is almost limited to the outer cell (Figure 5H–I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5H-I.

claim: T cell interactions with cell-in-cell tumors were insufficient to induce caspase 3/7 activity in the inner cell, leaving it intact and alive.
source: While these interactions were sufficient to kill single tumor cells, they were insufficient to induce caspase 3/7 activity in the inner cell, leaving it intact and alive (Figure 5G–J, and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by caspase 3/7 activity assay data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Cell-in-cell formation tumors survived longer and at higher concentrations of free radicals and chemotherapies compared to their parental cell lines.
source: Lastly, we compared the sensitivity of single-tumor cells to that of cell-in-cell tumors to additional antibiotics including free radicals and chemotherapies. Similar to our results with T cells, in all the tested compounds, cell-in-cell formation tumors survived longer and at higher concentrations compared to their parental cell lines (Figure 5K and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 5K and supplementary figures.

claim: Each cell type in the cell-in-cell formation maintained its cytoplasm, and no mix between fluorescent colors was detected.
source: Thus, we incubated tumor cells whose cytosols were labeled with either Wasabi or tdTomato with tumor-reactive T cells. Confocal analysis indicated that each cell type in the cell-in-cell formation maintained its cytoplasm, and no mix between colors was detected (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Long-term follow-up of cell dissemination from cell-in-cell structures indicated that each cell maintains its initial single labelling color.
source: Furthermore, long-term follow-up of cell dissemination from this structure indicated that each cell maintains its initial single labelling color (Figure 6—video 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse video microscopy.

claim: Blocking ROCK almost completely prevented T cell-mediated cell-in-cell formation.
source: Given the similarity of this formation to entosis, we used ROCK inhibitor, which is the key regulator of this process. Indeed, blocking ROCK almost completely prevented T cell-mediated cell-in-cell formation (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: There was no increase or changes in the cellular localization of phosphorylated β catenin, E-cadherin, and phosphorylated integrin β1 in cell-in-cell structures.
source: However, we observed no increase or changes in the cellular localization of phosphorylated β catenin, E-cadherin, and phosphorylated integrin β1 (26) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) suggesting other mediators promote this entosis.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: There was no reduction in cell-in-cell formation upon blocking of E- and N- cadherins, or inhibition of Wnt signaling.
source: Furthermore, there was no reduction in cell-in-cell formation upon blocking of E- and N- cadherins, or inhibition of Wnt signaling (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: Disruption of actin filaments, blocking of mRNA synthesis or protein production completely abrogated tumor cells' capacity to form a cell-in-cell formation.
source: In sharp contrast, disruption of actin filaments, blocking of mRNA synthesis or protein production completely abrogated tumor cells' capacity to form a cell-in-cell formation, suggesting that the structure requires de novo synthesis of genes (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D-E using various inhibitors.

claim: KEGG analysis indicated that multiple signaling cascades, including the JAK/STAT3 axis and FGF-receptors downstream pathways, are enriched in cell-in-cell formation generated in vivo.
source: KEGG analysis further indicated that multiple signaling cascades, including the JAK/STAT3 axis and FGF-receptors downstream pathways, are enriched in cell-in-cell formation generated in vivo, with approximately 80 significantly elevated genes relating to these pathways (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, ).
evidence: This is supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: EGR1 and STAT3 expression was significantly elevated in cell-in-cell tumors.
source: Indeed, EGR1 and STAT3 expression was significantly elevated in cell-in-cell tumors (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Both mice and human tumors incubated with reactive T cells had elevated their p-STAT3 levels, in comparison to untreated tumor cells.
source: Both mice and human tumors incubated with reactive T cells had elevated their p-STAT3 levels, in comparison to untreated tumor cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting this mechanism is conserved across species.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Overexpression of either STAT3 or EGR1 was sufficient to induce cell-in-cell formation without additional stimulation.
source: Overexpression of either STAT3 or EGR1 was sufficient to induce cell-in-cell formation without additional stimulation (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Cells overexpressing STAT3 or EGR1 were significantly more resistant to killing by CD8+ T cell, compared to sham transfected cells.
source: Furthermore, these cells were significantly more resistant to killing by CD8+ T cell, compared to sham transfected cells (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Inhibition of STAT3 and EGR1, but not MAPK3 and EGR2, significantly abrogated the capacity of tumor cells to form cell-in-cell structures upon incubation with IFNγ-stimulated T cells and with T cell secreted granules.
source: Inhibition of STAT3 and EGR1, but not MAPK3 and EGR2, significantly abrogated the capacity of tumor cells to form cell-in-cell structures upon incubation with IFNγ-stimulated T cells and with T cell secreted granules (Figure 6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Inhibition of STAT3, or EGR pathway, completely prevented cell-in-cell formation upon incubation with reactive T cells or T cell-secreted granules.
source: We found that inhibition of STAT3, or EGR pathway, completely prevented cell-in-cell formation upon incubation with reactive T cells or T cell-secreted granules (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using small molecule inhibitors shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Injection of Stattic prior to administration of immunotherapy partially restored the responsiveness of tumors that re-occur following immunotherapies.
source: We found, however, that injection of Stattic prior to administration of immunotherapy partially restored the responsiveness of tumors that re-occur following immunotherapies (Figure 6K–L).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 6K-L.

claim: Relapsed melanoma following treatment with pembrolizumab shares the majority of neoantigen with their corresponding primary tumors.
source: Zaretsky JM. et al. found that relapsed melanoma following treatment with pembrolizumab shares the majority of neoantigen with their corresponding primary tumors (Zaretsky et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Non-small cells carcinoma (NSCC) relapsed following treatment with anti-PD1 and CTLA-4 checkpoint blockade bear similar neoantigen load, with only a relatively small number of putative deleted clones.
source: Consistently, Anagnostou V. et al. found that non-small cells carcinoma (NSCC) relapsed following treatment with anti-PD1 and CTLA-4 checkpoint blockade bear similar neoantigen load, with only a relatively small number of putative deleted clones (Anagnostou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Three out of four basal cell carcinomas patients treated with pembrolizumab exhibited similar neoantigen burden.
source: In a recent study, Yost et al. demonstrated replenishment of T cell clones in basal cell carcinomas patients treated with pembrolizumab. Interestingly, three out of four analysed patients exhibited similar neoantigen burden (Yost et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Cell-in-cell structures generate multiple membrane layers, thus reducing the probability of compounds' internalization leading to increased tumor-cell survival.
source: Here, we found that tumor cells escape T-cell-based immunotherapies by forming a transient cell-in-cell structure, and not by immunoediting. These structures generate multiple membrane layers, thus reducing the probability of compounds' internalization leading to increased tumor-cell survival.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The present cell-in-cell structure is triggered predominantly by reactive T cells, rather than glucose and nutrient starvation, mitosis, or loss of adherence.
source: Although the present cell-in-cell structural falls within the definition entosis, it differs in several key elements: First, it is triggered predominantly by reactive T cells, rather than glucose and nutrient starvation (Hamann et al., 2017), mitosis (Durgan et al., 2017), or loss of adherence (Overholtzer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to published literature on entosis.

claim: The cell-in-cell structure requires de novo synthesis of genes regulated by STAT3, and not through β-catenin signaling.
source: Additionally, it requires de novo synthesis of genes regulated by STAT3, and not through β-catenin signaling (Overholtzer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using inhibitors and gene expression analysis.

claim: The cell-in-cell structure described is reversible and only rarely leads to cell cannibalism and apoptosis.
source: Most importantly, the structure described here is reversible and only rarely leads to cell cannibalism and apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging showing dissemination of cells from the structure.

claim: Only tumor cells that are capable to undergo 'spontaneous' entosis due to loss of cell adhesion can form cell-in-cell structure following interactions with reactive T cells.
source: We found that only tumor cells that are capable to undergo 'spontaneous' entosis due to loss of cell adhesion, can form cell-in-cell structure following interactions with reactive T cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that hematopoietic cells do not form these structures.

claim: Hematopoietic cells do not undergo 'spontaneous' or T-cell-mediated entosis but rather emperipolesis.
source: In general, hematopoietic cells do no undergo entosis but rather emperipolesis (Krishna and Overholtzer, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Even in a model system where all the 'breaks' on T cell activity are removed, tumor cells may activate a STAT3 transcriptional program, which promotes spatial architecture impenetrable to cytotoxic mediators.
source: This work also highlights a theoretical limitation of anti-tumor immunity, as even in a model system where all the 'breaks' on T cell activity are removed, tumor cells may activate a STAT3 transcriptional program, which promotes spatial architecture impenetrable to cytotoxic mediators.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Immune-mediated entosis should be inhibited prior to immunotherapy in order to reduce tumor resistance to subsequent drugs.
source: Here, we suggest that immune-mediated entosis should be inhibited prior to immunotherapy in order to reduce tumor resistance to subsequent drugs.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings with Stattic treatment.
